entries.title: Efficient and Variation-Tolerant Tree Inference via Compact and Scalable Mapping in Analog CAMs
entries.abstract: Tree-based machine learning methods are widely adopted for their interpretability and state-of-the-art accuracy on tabular data. These methods face efficiency challenges on conventional architectures due to irregular memory access patterns during tree traversal. Prior work uses analog CAM to accelerate tree traversal, but inefficient mapping requires exponentially more analog CAM columns as tree depth increases. Accuracy is also degraded by device non-idealities such as programming variations and soft decision boundaries. To address these challenges, we propose ACTIVAR, a compact variation-tolerant tree implementation in a dense analog CAM array via software-hardware codesign. On the software side, we introduce an analog-CAM-aware compact tree model that employs hierarchical subtrees with shared features to maximize hardware utilization. This dense mapping introduces redundancy, improving both model accuracy and hardware defect tolerance. Additionally, we develop Variation-Enhanced Training, which utilizes a fuzzy overlap boundary strategy to build models resilient to analog noise. On the hardware side, we design a FeFET-based analog CAM cell with a driver to sharpen decision thresholds and implement a pipelined multi-core architecture to optimize throughput and energy consumption. Across 13 classification and regression datasets, ACTIVAR maintains near-software-level accuracy while reducing hardware overhead by up to 99% compared with prior analog-CAM-based soft-tree designs. Under realistic hardware noise conditions, ACTIVAR limits accuracy degradation to just 3.7% on the MNIST dataset, whereas baseline models suffer a catastrophic 49.6% drop. Furthermore, the ACTIVAR architecture achieves energy efficiency gains ranging from 10⁴ to 10⁶ times over commercial general-purpose processors, establishing it as a highly efficient solution for high-capacity machine learning at the edge.

entries.title: CAVQS: Context-Aware Variational Quantum Circuit Synthesis via Unitary Redistribution and Dynamic Reconstruction
entries.abstract: Variational quantum circuit synthesis jointly searches circuit structure and continuous parameters to reduce costly two-qubit gates, but block-based workflows typically instantiate blocks independently, limiting simplification across block boundaries. Moreover, fully unitary synthesis does not exploit opportunities created by permitted output measurements and classical feedforward. We present CAVQS, a context-aware variational synthesis framework that combines unitary redistribution and dynamic reconstruction. First, CAVQS uses QR decomposition to transfer unitary factors between overlapping blocks, preserving the overall transformation while reshaping local synthesis targets to enable cross-block reductions. Second, for blocks that precede permitted terminal measurements, CAVQS constructs ancilla-free dynamic implementations with a CNOT-budgeted pre-measurement search and analytic branch-unitary construction, thereby minimizing expected CNOT cost. Across random-circuit targets, CAVQS reduces mean two-qubit gate counts by 28.79%-42.52%, 2.05%-52.62%, and 30.51%-74.64% relative to QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN, respectively, on common successful instances. On 4–6-qubit quantum algorithm benchmarks, the corresponding reductions are 27.27%-36.77%, 20.65%-69.10%, and 36.31%-71.88%, respectively.

entries.title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)
entries.abstract: The global deployment of autonomous AI agents within and across organisations exceeds the governance infrastructure available to constrain it. Agent communication and authentication protocols, principally the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent Protocol, are maturing quickly, but maturity at the protocol layer does not produce legal legibility at the governance layer. Runtime enforcement written by the deploying organisation fixes the resources an AI agent can reach, not the authority under which it acts. Legal legibility is the capacity of a legal system to recognise, interpret and regulate activity by mapping it onto legal personhood, property, rights and liabilities. Existing (analogue) legal infrastructure cannot supply it for autonomous deployment. The resulting deficit is bidirectional. It concerns the attribution of liability when an AI agent causes harm, and the allocation of rights, including data and economic rights, generated by agentic activity and by the AI agent itself as a source of value and form of property. This paper characterises that deficit as the legal attribution gap, a material and unaddressed risk to economies, organisations and citizens that is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployment. The paper describes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), in which AI systems and data assets are registered as legal objects anchored to one or more identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments and evaluated at runtime. Each smart legal instrument can carry a legal context clause, through which the legislation, regulation and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act are given practical and legal effect in that evaluation. Infrastructure of this kind is a precondition for the continued function of any legal, property and economic system with both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.

entries.title: Atlas: Accelerating Quantum FTQC Compilation with Optimized Algebraic Rotation Synthesis
entries.abstract: As fault-tolerant quantum computing emerges, Clifford+T gate basis becomes a popular choice where we need to decompose single-qubit rotation gates into gates in this gate basis. Quantum rotation synthesis may lead to remarkable overhead in quantum circuit compilation. Considering variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) applications as an example, a conventional UCCSD ansatz in quantum chemistry can generate O(n⁴) rotations for n qubits. Each optimization iteration updates the rotation angles, making rotation synthesis a recurring cost that can delay the VQE training loop. We identify two sources of delay in rotation synthesis: redundant computation during synthesis and uneven synthesis times that leave workers waiting for slow requests. Atlas addresses these costs with three optimizations: search pruning skips invalid synthesis candidates through statistical inference; adaptive arithmetic avoid unnecessary high-overhead big integer/float arithmetic when decomposing the target rotation gate; batch scheduling fills the gap between the synthesis time of varied rotations. Across various benchmarks, synthesis method, and compilation machines, Atlas can consistently accelerate the rotation synthesis process by up to 12.65x.

entries.title: Compiling Constraints into Neuromorphic Ising Machines
entries.abstract: Most practical combinatorial optimization problems involve constraints, and an Ising machine that flips one spin at a time can respect them only through energy penalties that raise barriers between feasible solutions. Here we show that a higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine can enforce constraints through programmable transitions rather than penalties. In an autoencoder-like architecture, each inner-layer neuron represents a move, a family of multi-spin transitions that maps every feasible state to another feasible state, receives the energy change of its move through connections that outer-layer neurons multiplicatively switch on or off, and updates the state through the same connections. A compiler turns constraints into this wiring with a number of auxiliary clauses that grows only polynomially for parity, cardinality, one-hot, partition and permutation constraints. Restricting the search to feasible states reduces constraint handling to move design, and we show that the fastest-annealing moves are not those that mix fastest but those that lower the deepest energy barriers, and that moves chosen from the objective lower them further than random ones. On third-order graph matching, the machine needs orders of magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines. Configured as a sampler on a field-programmable gate array, it decodes the surface code with maximum-likelihood accuracy up to code distance 15 within 52 μs per shot and, under noisy syndrome measurements, decodes in real time for millisecond measurement rounds up to distance 9 with fewer logical errors than belief-propagation decoders.
entries.comment: 41 pages, 6 figures, with Supplementary Information (46 pages)

entries.title: RE-CAM: Readout-Enhanced Content-Addressable Memory for Quantitative Similarity Search
entries.abstract: Similarity search is essential to many applications but incurs massive data movement when executed on conventional architectures. Content-addressable memory (CAM) is a promising hardware substrate, as it allows similarity search directly in the CAM array, minimizing data movement and offering both low latency and high energy efficiency. However, conventional CAM array readout produces only binary match results, discarding quantitative similarity information that could be further exploited. Extracting this information requires interpreting the CAM array output voltage that evolves during a CAM search, making the sensing timestamp a crucial design variable alongside the reference voltage and decoding parameter. In this work, we propose RE-CAM, a readout enhancement framework for CAM that is agnostic to memory technology and application, enabling CAM array readout to approximate linear and nonlinear functions with one CAM search. By reusing the comparators to sense the time-varying output voltage multiple times, jointly optimizing the three design variables under system constraints and hardware nonidealities, and co-designing the optimization algorithm and reconfigurable hardware, RE-CAM achieves accurate approximation with low energy and area overhead without introducing a readout throughput bottleneck. Across linear, piecewise-linear, sigmoid, and exponential functions, RE-CAM reduces normalized root mean square error by 10.89% to 24.34% for general approximation and 29.43% to 46.73% when exploiting dataset distribution, compared to a shared uniform-reference ADC baseline with the same comparison budget. Relative to the same baseline, RE-CAM also achieves 8× higher search throughput while reducing energy per search and area by 47% and 39%, respectively.

entries.title: Crisis Governance at the Joints. Mapping the Ethical and Societal Territory of Crisis Management Technologies: The Case of Human-Swarm Teaming
entries.abstract: Crisis and disaster governance increasingly relies on technologies that sense, classify and act faster than humans can. Drone swarms coordinated with human operators, known as human-swarm teaming, provide a productive case to review the field of crisis governance. They promise better situational awareness in disaster response, but they also raise questions about human control, responsibility, surveillance, triage, dual use and public legitimacy. This report maps the ethical and societal territory that HST opens up. It unpacks this territory with a 3i-framework, the Interface, where operators and swarms work together, the Infrastructure, where organisations distribute tasks, decisions and blame, and the Imaginary, where law, policy and shared societal assumptions define what a crisis is and which interventions it justifies. The central claim is that these concerns cannot be addressed one level at a time. Many of the most pressing problems, such as responsibility gaps and the erosion of meaningful human control, arise at the joints between levels, through four translations, habits harden, routines become stories, principles become procedures, and procedures become prompts. Drawing on a critical review of literature across philosophy of technology, political theory, moral psychology, philosophy of mind, AI ethics, and critical disaster and security studies, the report develops this framework, illustrates it with two worked examples, and derives design and governance implications and a set of questions for developers, emergency organisations and policymakers.

entries.title: CAIMS: Scalable Cross-Array In-Memory Search
entries.abstract: Search, especially top-k similarity search, plays a vital role in many applications, but its performance can be severely limited by memory access overhead. In-memory search (IMS), an alternative to CPU/GPU-based approaches, exploits massive parallelism within a content-addressable memory (CAM) array to perform search in situ and provides both low latency and high energy efficiency. However, the capacity of a single CAM array is often insufficient for modern workloads, requiring data to be distributed across multiple arrays. Deploying scalable top-k similarity search across multiple CAM arrays poses a fundamental problem that existing designs fail to address: how to accurately and efficiently reduce local binary match results to global top-k results. This work introduces CAIMS, a cross-array IMS framework that is agnostic to memory technologies and applications, enabling scalable and efficient top-k similarity search while preserving accuracy. To enable accurate top-k result reduction, CAIMS leverages the existing threshold match functionality with a combined offline and online parameter selection approach to transform local binary match results that lack globally comparable similarity information into global coarse-grained similarity scores. To further improve efficiency, CAIMS conducts hierarchical reduction and transfers only the selection results and necessary control signals with lightweight local peripherals. Implemented on a 3D NAND Flash model and demonstrated using the retrieval phase of retrieval-augmented generation, CAIMS improves throughput by up to 22.3×/10.1× and energy efficiency by 426.6×/23.7× compared to the server-class CPU baseline and prior 3D NAND Flash accelerators, respectively, while maintaining comparable accuracy.

entries.title: ReCIM-HD: A 40 nm On-Device Learning Accelerator with Hyperdimensional Computing via Importance-Based Hybrid Digital-ReRAM CIM
entries.abstract: ReCIM-HD is an on-device learning (ODL) accelerator that integrates gradient-free hyperdimensional computing (HDC) with resistive RAM (ReRAM)-based analog compute-in-memory (CIM). ReCIM-HD introduces three key techniques: (1) ultra-low-power HDC-based edge ODL without costly back-propagation operations; (2) non-volatile ReRAM-based storage for class hypervectors and CIM similarity search, enabling energy-efficient inference and power-gating during idle periods without data loss; and (3) a hybrid digital-analog CIM inference flow that protects a small accuracy-critical subset digitally to preserve accuracy. Additionally, it employs a Kronecker HD encoder (KE) to reduce encoding overhead and a customized instruction set architecture (ISA) to support flexible programmability. Fabricated in 40 nm, ReCIM-HD achieves 44.17 TOPS/W (hybrid mode) and 75.8 TOPS/W (ReRAM CIM mode), delivering up to 20.1x higher energy efficiency than the state-of-the-art accelerator.

entries.title: Breaking the Myth of Four-Tier Stacked Transistors for Logic: an Investigation from Process to Device and Block-Level PPA
entries.abstract: For the first time, this work evaluated whether 4-tier stacked transistors can translate the straightforward density gains into realistic chip-level scaling benefits. A practical dual-sided 4-tier transistor-stacking CFFET (Flipped CFET-to-CFET) process was proposed, on which a DTCO framework spanning standard-cell design, local interconnects, RO analysis, and physical implementation was built under 2A node design rules. The CFFET was also benchmarked with its 2-tier transistor-stacking counterparts FFET. Among CFFET configurations, the best-performing Symmetric Power still lags FFET by 11.2% in RO frequency due to the complex MOL parasitics. At the block level, CFFET reduces the Ibex RISC-V core area by only 12.8% (far below the 40% nominal cell-height reduction), while running 10.9% slower at iso-power. We further introduced a novel Tetris-like cell stitching to minimize the area overhead, which allows non-rectangular cell design and recovers 7.4% area in a 1-bit ALU design. An optimized NanoStack CFFET was finally proposed, inspired by previous work. This work indicates that straightforward vertical 4-tier stacking proves insufficient to guarantee enough PPA benefits, though the resulting design insights may guide future advanced architectures.

entries.title: A Probabilistic Behavioral RTL Simulation Framework for Probabilistic Compute Fabrics
entries.abstract: Coupled oscillator Ising hardware can produce different solution qualities across repeated runs of the same problem, while a deterministic behavioral model used for the design yields a single outcome under fixed conditions. Capturing this stochastic variability during design time is essential for evaluating how closely simulation reflects silicon behavior. This work presents a probabilistic behavioral RTL simulation framework that introduces Gaussian timing variation into coupling delays. This variation changes oscillator timing during evolution, producing different outcomes across runs while retaining the existing chip control and readout blocks. The framework is evaluated against measurements from two chips: a 28-nm CMOS chip with 66 spins and a 16-nm FinFET chip with 49 spins, using 250 problems run 100 times repetitively. Compared with deterministic simulation, the model reduces the average absolute gap between sorted simulation and silicon outcomes by 14.0% and 28.4% on the two chips, respectively. These results demonstrate that a simple behavioral timing variation model can be a useful tool for designing and verifying probabilistic computing chips.

entries.title: Optical Neural Networks Should Be Evaluated by Function, Not Only Physics
entries.abstract: Optical neural networks (ONNs) are attracting significant attention as alternative platforms for machine learning (ML). In an ONN, an optical module often takes over part of the computation inside a digital ML pipeline. How much of the task does the optical module itself perform, and how much does it contribute to any claimed system-level advantages, such as throughput or energy? This paper offers a simple, function-oriented evaluation methodology. Whatever its internal physics, the optical module appears to the surrounding digital pipeline as a mapping between real-valued tensors. We therefore evaluate it in three steps: (i) define its boundary in the pipeline, as real-valued tensors in and out; (ii) replace it with standard digital modules to identify those that match the optical system's performance on the same task and metric; and (iii) state system-level claims, such as speed or energy, per inference against the performance-matched digital module. We summarize steps (i) and (ii) in an Expressivity Card and demonstrate its use on published ONN systems. This helps isolate the optical module's contribution and provides a concrete digital reference for assessing its claimed system-level advantages, without the need to understand the physics. While we focus on optical systems as the most prominent example, the same approach applies to any physical analog computing platform used in ML, wherever a physical module takes over part of a digital pipeline.

entries.title: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
entries.abstract: We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6× and 238× lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3× (Willow) and 4.9-204× (SI1000, p = 10⁻³) lower logical error rate.

entries.title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model
entries.abstract: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. We propose a residual-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework for lightweight trajectory selection with a frozen world model and a fixed candidate bank. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.

entries.title: 3D-VASE: Volumetric-Aware Scalable and Efficient Multi-Layer Design Synthesis for 3D-Printed Microfluidics
entries.abstract: Additive manufacturing (3D printing) enables complex multi-layer microfluidic devices, but the physical synthesis of passive-flow designs remains a key bottleneck. In such systems, designers must encode timing synchronization and target dosing directly into channel geometry, even though the available routing space across multiple 3D layers is often highly congested, which makes scaling to complex designs difficult. Existing approaches formulate placement, routing, and fluidic constraints as a single monolithic optimization, leading to combinatorial explosion and poor performance on complex designs. This paper presents a volumetric-aware two-stage synthesis framework that decouples global structure from routing detail. A Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) model first computes a compact multi-layer placement, followed by a dynamic 3D routing engine that enforces timing and volumetric constraints during path construction. To further improve routability in dense layouts, we introduce a hierarchical conflict resolution strategy combining local rip-up-and-reroute with controlled global expansion. Experimental results show that, under timing and volumetric constraints, 3D-VASE consistently improves synthesis speed and, in most test cases, also improves layout quality. Notably, for difficult large-scale cases where prior methods often failed to return any solution within the time limit, 3D-VASE produces feasible high-quality layouts within practical runtimes. These advances enable fast, iterative design-space exploration for complex 3D-printed microfluidic systems.
entries.comment: Accepted for publication in the 32nd Asia and South Pacific Design Automation Conference (ASP-DAC 2027)

entries.title: Countering Anion Inhibition of Laccase Electron Transfer: Electrostatic Design, Charge-Transfer Dynamics on a Superconducting Quantum Processor, and Its Limits
entries.abstract: Hydroxide at neutral-to-alkaline pH and halides inhibit fungal laccases and limit their use in wastewater treatment. From GFN2-xTB cluster models of Trametes versicolor laccase (PDB 1GYC) we build a four-site Hubbard model of the His454-T3A-T3B-His452 junction of the trinuclear copper cluster and execute its charge-transfer dynamics on the Euro-Q-Exa quantum computer (IQM, 8 qubits, Trotterized circuits with Pauli twirling; 726 jobs). The charge-transfer frequency is measured to 3-5 meV, reproducibly over nine days and across changes of the device qubit map: hydroxide raises the charge-transfer energy of the crystal-geometry model by 92.0 +/- 2.2 meV (exact 87) and exceeds fluoride by 10.1 +/- 1.8 meV. A screen of charged probes in three dielectric models identifies Y116E; in the probe model the hardware resolves a reduction of the hydroxide penalty by 74 +/- 7 meV and of the halide penalty by 64 +/- 5 meV, acting on the site-energy gap rather than on the coupling. A real Glu116 (five conformers) with PROPKA protonation states and the coupled Asp456 gives a realistic reduction of 10-30 meV, with the same sign in 28 of 28 model combinations; the direction and ordering are the prediction, rate factors only an illustration. Scanning the on-site repulsion reverses the sign of the hydroxide effect, and a one-electron Hartree model reproduces the reversal: the measured dynamics is effectively single-particle. On a Fermi-Hubbard benchmark the hardware does not resolve electron correlation; it would need a contrast loss below 0.13 percent per CZ gate instead of the measured 0.34-0.54 percent.
entries.comment: Main text 17 pages, supporting informations 13 pages

entries.title: A Copper-Inducible Yeast Biosensor with Bioluminescent Readout: Mathematical Modeling, Experimental Validation, and Photodetector Coupling for Molecular Communication in IoBNT
entries.abstract: Engineered living biosensors constitute promising model organisms for bringing Molecular Communications (MC) closer to practical applications. However, challenges associated with their development and characterization have resulted in the relevant literature being limited in the MC domain,. In this paper, we contribute in this direction by leveraging engineered yeast as a basis to detect heavy metals such as copper. The biosensor's development is supported by a validated mathematical characterization and analysis for possible integration in an MC system. Different from the existing literature, mathematical representations of the major biological processes within the yeast copper detoxification pathway are integrated into a comprehensive framework that predicts the time evolution of the CUP1 gene, which is treated as the system output. In the engineered circuit, CUP1 was replaced with GFP, therefore making GFP fluorescence the final system output. Experimental analysis including mRNA transcript quantification and fluorometric measurements, validate the GFP reporting model to a satisfactory degree. This establishes the proposed model as a useful tool for virtual experimentation and the developed testbed as a suitable platform for further engineering of yeast-based copper sensors. The theoretical analysis is further extended by incorporating a self-sustained bioluminescent reporter for yeast, replacing GFP and enabling optical output without external light excitation. The optical response is coupled to a photodetector model, rendering the system suitable for integration into mobile monitoring devices such as Smart Pills. The presented characterization of the yeast receiver as a copper biosensor, constitutes the first step towards the development and characterization of a complete end-to-end MC based system for gut theranostics after coupling with suitable engineered probiotic senders.

entries.title: Automated-Truck Penetration Shapes Human Drivers' Car-Following Margins Near Motorway Ramps: A Driving-Simulator Study
entries.abstract: Automated-vehicle dedicated lanes (AVDLs) are proposed as transitional infrastructure for mixed traffic, but their effect near ramps, and that of automated trucks, on the human drivers sharing the road has rarely been observed. In a mixed-design driving-simulator experiment, 63 drivers were assigned to one of four layouts (an AVDL extending beyond, coinciding with, or ending inside a 1.5-km ramp weaving section, or no AVDL) and drove at four automated-truck penetration levels from 20% to 80%. Linear mixed-effects models with participant random effects and multiplicity control were used. Higher penetration reduced the share of car-following time at gaps below 1.5 s from 28.5% to 18.1% (Holm-adjusted p =.006). This was explained by leader composition: drivers spent 8% of following time behind a truck at 20% penetration and 48% at 80%, kept longer gaps behind trucks, and did not change their gaps within leader type. AVDL layout had no detectable effect on safety margins, rear-end conflict rates, travel time or speed (differences bounded within plus or minus 5 s per section) and no significant effect on workload. Between-driver differences accounted for 52% to 77% of the variance in the main outcomes. Mixed-traffic models should therefore represent human car-following as leader-type-dependent and heterogeneous.

entries.title: Noise Characterization and Robust Signal Detection in Yeast Pheromone Molecular Communication
entries.abstract: A critical aspect of Molecular Communications (MC) is the implementation of signal detection policies amidst noise. To date, noise characterizations within the MC field have predominantly drawn from methodologies found in wireless communications literature. In this study, we diverge from existing MC research by utilizing a newly developed experimental platform that employs yeast, allowing us to consider more realistic noise characterizations based on the relevant signaling pathways. We propose suitable signal detection mechanisms tailored to this experimental setup, which focuses on yeast cell-to-cell communications. Our analysis identifies gene transcription as the primary source of noise, and we utilize a Markov birth-death process model with Poisson arrivals and departures to characterize it. The noisy expression of the FUS1 gene is best represented using a mixed Gaussian distribution model. This model serves as a foundation for evaluating the performance of Maximum Likelihood Detection mechanisms in terms of Bit Error Rate (BER) for both symbol-by-symbol and sequence transmission schemes. Error analysis indicates that appropriate adjustments to the signal threshold can reduce errors to as low as 10%, which is not negligible. In contrast, the detection of symbol sequences demonstrates enhanced error performance, achieving error rates as low as 0.4%, albeit at the cost of increased computational complexity.

entries.title: MASQ: Measurement-Adaptive Sampling for Near-Clifford Quantum Error Correction Circuits
entries.abstract: Classical sampling of quantum error correction (QEC) circuits supports fault-tolerant protocol evaluation, but estimating rare logical failures requires many independent shots. Frame-active-state simulators isolate non-stabilizer information in a dense active-state vector, yet dense-state processing remains exponential in the active width. This paper presents MASQ, an exact measurement-adaptive sampler for near-Clifford QEC circuits based on selective materialization of non-Clifford rotations. At each measurement boundary, MASQ materializes only rotations in a measurement-relevant closure capturing direct and indirect non-commuting dependencies, deferring the rest to limit active-state expansion. Stabilizer-assisted elimination further removes rotations certified to be invisible to all future measurements. A circuit-dependent schedule is computed once and shared across shots, while adaptive caching of conditional Born probabilities and batched execution reduce repeated sampling work while preserving the measurement-record distribution. Across 19 QEC benchmarks, MASQ reduces peak active width by up to 40 active virtual qubits and achieves up to 8,098-fold CPU throughput speedup over Clifft on multi-round circuits.
entries.comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, and 1 table. This paper has been accepted for publication at DATE 2027

entries.title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
entries.abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.
entries.comment: Accepted in IEEE Annual Congress on Artificial Intelligence of Things (IEEE AIoT) 2026. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter

entries.title: Threat Landscape of Vibe Coding and the Road to Secure Autonomy
entries.abstract: Vibe coding is reshaping software development, enabling faster implementation and allowing individuals with limited programming experience to describe requirements in natural language while AI agents write, test, and deploy the code. As these agents evolve into autonomous systems that execute commands, manage dependencies, access cloud resources, and interact with other agents, their security risks extend beyond incorrect code to actions with direct consequences for software systems. Although research on these risks is expanding, it remains fragmented across areas including prompt injection, insecure code generation, supply-chain attacks, and human factors, with limited consensus on terminology, threat assumptions, and evaluation. This paper consolidates emerging research through the lens of the vibe coding workflow. We establish a reference architecture, characterise six levels of agent autonomy, and develop a threat model centred on five trust boundaries spanning developers, AI models, tools, cloud infrastructure, and the wider software ecosystem. Building on this foundation, we propose a taxonomy of twenty-one threats across nine classes. For each threat, we review the available evidence, assess proposed defences, and identify limitations. Our analysis highlights that risks increase with agents' operational authority, while most defences rely on model judgement and address isolated threats. Finally, we identify eleven research challenges, including enforceable limits on agent authority and shared benchmarks and methodologies for assessing vibe coding security.
entries.comment: 35 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables, Submitted to ACM Computing Surveys

entries.title: Surrogate-Assisted Compact-Model Extraction for SKY130 CMOS at 77 K
entries.abstract: Cryogenic circuit design requires compact transistor models that reproduce measured low-temperature behavior and run in standard circuit simulators. We fit BSIM4 parameters to measured I-V curves of SkyWater 130 nm (SKY130) transistors at 77 K using a neural surrogate of NGSpice. The surrogate maps compact-model parameters and device geometry to the complete set of output and transfer characteristics. Extraction is a bounded least-squares search: a bank of NGSpice simulations supplies initial candidates, finite differences of the surrogate supply the local Jacobian, and NGSpice re-simulates the resulting cards before selection. On 18 measured geometries, we compare a search over seven card parameters with a search over 43 parameters selected by NGSpice sensitivity. Relative to NGSpice re-simulations of the previously released cards, the two searches reduce the in-sample mean relative root-mean-square error (RRMS) by 17% and 26%, respectively. The 43-parameter search has the lower overall error, but the seven-parameter search has the lower mean on high-bias curves, and some individual curves have higher error than with the released cards under both searches.

entries.title: SCOPE: A Physical Execution Latency-Guided Quantum Circuit Compilation Framework
entries.abstract: Quantum computing requires compilers to translate algorithms represented in the quantum circuit model into unitary operations supported by physical devices. Limited coherence time makes physical execution latency an important compilation objective. Gate fusion can shorten pulses, but gate count and depth do not capture fused targets' control demands. Evaluating every candidate with quantum optimal control (QOC) would embed pulse optimization in structural search. We present Schmidt-guided Compilation for Optimized Pulse Execution (SCOPE), driven by an operator Schmidt time surrogate. The target's angular distance from product operators measures the required nonlocal change; dividing it by a coupling-limited evolution-rate bound gives a lower bound on exact implementation time. Trace-angle and waveform constraints complete block scores for critical-path evaluation during genetic search. Local QOC determines final pulse durations. Under a numerical nearest-neighbor control model, all 104 results across 13 instances from four application families have shorter QOC critical-path durations than an adapted efficient pulse generation framework with advanced synthesis for quantum circuits (EPOC). Using eight-run instance means, the equally weighted reduction is 42.50%, with a geometric mean speedup of 2.00. In a shared six-qubit quantum Fourier transform (QFT) ablation, time-surrogate guidance reduces mean QOC duration by 22.21% relative to gate-count guidance and 21.01% relative to depth guidance, validating the surrogate's joint use in fitness evaluation and mutation-region selection.

entries.title: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning
entries.abstract: Enterprise AI can now perform analytics, reporting, and data-driven workflows, yet the data foundations it relies on remain hard to operationalize: business meaning, relationships, metric definitions, and reporting conventions are absent from database schemas and scattered across undocumented systems and tribal knowledge. We introduce the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned context layer that makes existing enterprise data operational for AI without requiring a copy or transformation of the underlying warehouse. LCG bootstraps base semantics and relationships from the data itself, builds a concept graph that indexes business context as queries are served, writes durable semantic learnings from verified outcomes, and withdraws or re-earns context when later outcomes contradict prior routes. We evaluate LCG through text-to-SQL, a core data-reasoning task, on a transfer-aware split of three BIRD databases comprising 499 questions: 353 form the learning history and 146 are held out and never used to update the context layer. Bootstrapping alone improves overall accuracy by +4.6 percentage points. Learning only from the history raises accuracy on the untouched held-out transfer set by +22.6 points (95% CI [+14.4, +30.8]), exceeding five-shot retrieval from the same history by +12.3 points. Incremental learning reaches the one-shot endpoint within observed evaluation noise on every database. Ablating the graph changes held-out accuracy by at most one question per database but increases per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x: continually learned semantics drive accuracy, while the graph makes that context efficient to serve.
entries.comment: 22 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Continual Learning in the Era of Foundation Models and Embodied Agents. Data splits and annotations: https://github.com/varunagrawal2002/Living-Context-Graph

entries.title: Observable Spectral Framework for Noisy Amplitude Amplification: Stopping Stability and Correction
entries.abstract: Stopping rules for noisy amplitude amplification often rely on channel-specific success-probability formulas, limiting their transfer across noise mechanisms. We develop an observable spectral framework for stationary noisy standard amplitude amplification under explicit leading-mode, spectral-separation, and residual-control conditions. Within this class, the first amplification lobe has a damped-oscillatory leading component and a bounded non-leading contribution. We derive how frequency shift, damping, and observable phase offset displace the leading peak, and establish sampled-gap criteria for retaining the ideal integer stopping depth, certifying recalibration, or selecting a robust candidate window. In single-target Grover search, frequency and damping errors have stopping-coordinate sensitivities proportional to the search-space size, whereas phase offsets scale with its square root; residual modes can independently reverse the ordering of neighbouring depths. Analytical constructions, circuit simulations, finite-shot inference, and calibration-derived device-like trajectories examine these predictions and their operational limits. For a 64-element search, an a posteriori sampled-set check selects depth five over six, with success probability increasing from 0.595 to 0.626. The resulting theory links observable spectral dynamics to conditional integer stopping guarantees without requiring a separate microscopic channel solution.
entries.comment: 28 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables; includes 38-page supplementary material (10 figures). Submitted to EPJ Quantum Technology

entries.title: Response-Threshold Framework for First-Peak Preservation in Noisy Grover Search
entries.abstract: Grover search is executed only after integer iterations, so noise can alter the stopping decision even when a continuous first peak remains visible. We develop a response-threshold framework separating continuous peak motion, stroboscopic geometry, and the discrete sampled-success argmax. For a Drude-Lorentz environment, linearized HEOM supplies an a priori timing coefficient and sampled-probability differentials. The first-order layer is used as a conservative screen: well-separated points retain the nominal step, whereas near-threshold points escalate to finite-λ evaluation. Across 260 unique HEOM points drawn from five overlapping validation sets, it detects all 15 observed stopping changes with zero regret on the changed subset; its residual errors are 45 one-step-early calls on otherwise stable points; the 245-point stable subset has mean regret 4.42×10⁻³. An empirically validated two-stage workflow escalates every observed change while avoiding 160 of 260 unique full-HEOM propagations. Same-bath NZ2 reduces early calls. A heterogeneous three-qubit circuit exhibits three stopping-transition scales, each replicated across eight marked targets, and finite-shot recovery is 96.18% overall, with failures localized to a near-degenerate boundary at s=1.5. A depth-refined transfer test supports the predicted local quadratic timing-to-loss relation.

entries.title: Cyber-Secure Wearable, Ultra-Low-Power Networked Sensors for Soldier Health Monitoring: Insights from the CAPSARII project
entries.abstract: The CAPSARII project advances a cyber-secure, ultra-low-power wearable platform and Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) framework to support real-time monitoring of military personnel and data-driven decision support. The architecture integrates smart-textile sensing, a body/squad area mesh, edge-deployed AI on secure RISC-V microcontrollers, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning and comparative studies. Two representative use cases–pilot fatigue and warfighters operating in harsh environments–guide requirements, validation, and interface design (including HUD and haptic feedback). As an initial step toward embedded models, we benchmark stress classification on a public wearable dataset: tree-ensemble baselines achieve state-of-the-art performance for accuracy and F1 (e.g., XGBoost: Accuracy=0.901±0.023, F1=0.920±0.019), while a feature-based Transformer attains the highest AUC (0.963±0.025), informing feature-engineering and compression choices for edge deployment. Building on these results, CAPSARII employs HW/SW co-design, model compression (pruning, quantization, distillation), and precision tuning to meet stringent energy and memory budgets; it further investigates Processing-in-Memory accelerators for future efficiency gains. A structured gap analysis highlights the remaining challenges: establishing validation standards for physiological signal quality and textile durability; achieving low-latency, scalable BAN/SAN communications under mobility and interference; and deploying hybrid lightweight/post-quantum cryptography with robust device identity and side-channel resilience on constrained endpoints. By consolidating these elements into a coherent, secure IoBT stack, CAPSARII delineates a practical roadmap from laboratory baselines to mission-ready soldier monitoring in both training and operational scenarios.

entries.title: Discovering Programmatic Policies from Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Controllers
entries.abstract: Traffic signal control (TSC) is critical for mitigating urban congestion. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved strong performance by learning adaptive policies from traffic observations, but learned neural controllers are often opaque, structurally complex, and difficult to generalize across scenarios. We propose PPL-TSC, a programmatic policy learning framework that distills compact and human-readable TSC policies from DRL teachers. PPL-TSC formulates policy learning as an evolutionary search over phase utility functions (PUFs), which score candidate signal phases and select the highest-utility phase for execution. Each generation consists of four steps: policy generation, policy review, policy calibration, and policy evaluation. In the generation step, a large language model (LLM) acts as a semantics-aware evolutionary operator to propose and refine candidate PUFs. Generated PUFs are screened through explicit checks for syntactic validity, mathematical soundness, and consistency with TSC principles, with invalid ones repaired through iterative feedback. Valid PUFs are then calibrated to improve behavioral fidelity to the DRL teacher, and evaluated using a joint score combining teacher fidelity and traffic-control performance to select candidates for the next generation. Extensive experiments across diverse traffic scenarios and representative DRL-based controllers show that PPL-TSC produces compact and human-readable policies, achieves competitive performance for most teacher families, improves transfer generalization, and substantially reduces computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/ForrestXie9/PPL-TSC.

entries.title: CoSyDelay: Cognitive Symbolic Regression for Traffic Delay Estimation
entries.abstract: Trustworthy estimation of traffic delays at signalized intersections is critical for modern transportation systems, as it supports proactive traffic control for congestion mitigation. Existing analytical methods often rely on idealized assumptions that limit their accuracy under complex traffic conditions, whereas data-driven methods may achieve strong estimation performance but usually lack transparent structures, which reduces confidence in their practical application. To address these limitations, we propose CoSyDelay, a cognitive symbolic regression (SR) framework for automatically deriving explicit and physically consistent empirical delay estimation expressions (DEEs). Specifically, CoSyDelay decomposes intersection-level delay estimation into turning-movement-level subproblems, thereby reducing the complexity of the symbolic search. During DEE learning, CoSyDelay constructs domain-informed symbolic inputs from traffic variables. Large language models (LLMs) are employed as symbolic search operators to iteratively generate and refine candidate expression structures, whose movement-specific coefficients are subsequently calibrated using approach-level delay labels. A composite fitness function evaluates the learned DEEs jointly in terms of estimation accuracy and compliance with specified traffic-delay principles. Experimental results on multiple signalized intersections demonstrate that the resulting expressions achieve competitive estimation performance while maintaining physical consistency, thereby supporting trustworthy delay estimation. Source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ForrestXie9/CoSyDelay.

entries.title: HBF-EventLab: A Discrete-Event Simulator for Studying Host-Device Coordination in High Bandwidth Flash
entries.abstract: High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) combines NAND flash density with high-bandwidth accelerator connectivity, offering additional memory capacity for large language model inference. However, limited hardware availability makes it difficult to evaluate how host behavior and device resource constraints jointly affect HBF request processing. We present HBF-EventLab, an open-source, transaction-level discrete-event simulator based on the Open Compute Project HBF specification. HBF-EventLab connects host request dispatch, command admission, fragmented write assembly, read dispatch, NAND execution, and completion feedback within a shared event loop. It explicitly models distinct resource lifetimes and separates configurable scheduling policies from ordering and resource constraints, enabling controlled exploration of host-device coordination. Experiments show how resource limits, address interleaving, fragment arrival patterns, and scheduling policies affect write completion and request latency. The results highlight the need to consider resource limits and scheduling policies jointly, accounting for their interactions with write assembly and read eligibility. We also integrate HBF-EventLab with real GPU execution of Qwen3-0.6B, combining profiled GPU activity durations with simulated weight-access delays to estimate time to first token and time per output token, with logits and output tokens remaining bitwise identical to those from native GPU execution. HBF-EventLab provides a configurable foundation for studying HBF mechanisms, exploring scheduling policies, and assessing how HBF access delays affect application-level timing. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sjtu-epcc/HBF-EventLab.

entries.title: Developing JEEVHITAA: Designing and Evaluating a Human-Centered AI Ecosystem for Collective Care
entries.abstract: Health management is often a collective activity, involving family members and close relations in monitoring, interpreting, and coordinating care. Yet, most digital health technologies remain individual-centric, offering limited support for the distributed responsibilities and negotiated information sharing that characterize collective care. We present JEEVHITAA, a human-centered AI ecosystem designed to address this gap. Drawing on existing literature on collective health practices, we identify key requirements and translate them into a canonical ontology and a versioned data schema that underpin a mobile ecosystem integrating wearable data, role-aware sharing, granular access controls, auditable histories, and AI-assisted health summarization and verification. We first evaluated core system primitives using 1,000 ontology-driven synthetic care circles to test data visibility and information-processing workflows. We then conducted a controlled lab study with 13 subject–care-actor dyads (26 participants), combining task-based interactions, semi-structured interviews, the System Usability Scale, and component-level usability assessments. Findings indicate positive perceptions of usability and highlight the value of granular sharing and transparent information provenance. They also expose tensions between reciprocal transparency and surveillance, and between AI-mediated assistance and potentially intrusive notifications. We discuss implications for designing accountable, context-sensitive technologies that support collective care.
entries.comment: 38 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables, Preprint of a Submitted manuscript

entries.title: Shallow Clifford circuits on square lattices
entries.abstract: We study the depth of CZ circuits, Clifford state preparation, and Clifford unitary synthesis over the two-dimensional square lattice. A programmable circuit on a 2×k ladder (n=2k) implements an arbitrary CZ computation in depth at most 3n/2+3 up to reversal of both rails. This improves the best-known LNN (Linear Nearest-Neighbor)-compliant depth-(2n+2) construction by about 25%. For state preparation, we consider a Phase gate programmable -H-CNOT+P-LC- circuit and derive matching obstructions to attaining the CZ-span counting lower bound of 2⌈n/2⌉-1 for depth by the entangling gates. For cycle connectivity C_n, we prove that the minimum depth is exactly 2⌈n/2⌉-1 when n is not a multiple of four and 2⌈n/2⌉ when n = 4k. We construct a hole-free minimum-perimeter square-lattice patch with a Hamiltonian cycle for every even size, giving optimal-depth programmable circuits to implement Clifford states for all n = 4k+2. Exhaustive and heuristic searches address the remaining cases for n up to 256, and selected values up to 1,024 qubits. The improvement against comparable state-of-the-art, an LNN-compliant depth-(2n+2) solution, is about 50%. Finally, combining state synthesis circuits developed in this work with a known four-diagonal-stage decomposition gives rise to a depth 4n-4 for n = 4k+2 and depth 4n for n = 4k implementation of arbitrary Clifford unitaries. This improves the most relevant state-of-the-art, an LNN-compliant depth 7n-4 construction, by about 43%.

entries.title: Behavioral Assurance for Socially Deployed AI Agents
entries.abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.

entries.title: Q-Drive: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Control Framework for Nonlinear Vehicular Dynamics
entries.abstract: In this paper, we introduce Q-Drive, a hybrid quantum-classical control framework for nonlinear vehicular dynamics that integrates variational quantum circuits (VQCs) with classical optimization, encoding vehicle states into a quantum Hilbert space via angle embedding, applying a trainable quantum ansatz to generate control signals, and refining circuit parameters through gradient descent to minimize tracking error and control effort. The proposed Q-Drive is evaluated in two settings: Single-vehicle control of nonlinear bicycle dynamics and a decoupled multi-vehicle swarm scenario with fleet sizes ranging from N=2 to N=50, demonstrating that the approach achieves exceptionally low control effort, reduced by orders of magnitude compared to classical model predictive control (MPC) and linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) benchmarks in the single-vehicle case, with average per-vehicle control effort decreasing by over 60% from N=2 to N=50 in the swarm setting. Beyond empirical evaluation, we establish rigorous stability guarantees by constructing a composite Lyapunov function that jointly captures classical tracking dynamics and quantum-state purity. This analysis proves that the closed-loop system remains ultimately uniformly bounded under arbitrary road conditions, including inclined, rough, and curvilinear surfaces, as well as in the presence of quantum decoherence on the NISQ hardware, with explicit critical thresholds linking decoherence rates to environmental adversity. For the swarm extension, a theoretical bound is derived that shows that the average per-vehicle control effort decreases inversely with fleet size, in agreement with empirical observations. Q-Drive offers a promising direction for intelligent transportation systems by enabling robust, energy-efficient, and scalable vehicle control under complex real-world driving conditions.
entries.journalRef: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Vehicles, 12 November 2026

entries.title: Rethinking KV Caching for LLM Decode: Free-Space Optical KV Regeneration for Reduction of Memory Traffic
entries.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) decoding repeatedly reads the historical key-value (KV) cache, making multi-head attention (MHA) memory-bandwidth-bound. Caching layer-input activations instead halves historical-cache storage and traffic, but requires regenerating KV from each cached activation. On digital accelerators such as GPUs, this regeneration takes far longer than fetching the activation from HBM. The KV regeneration overhead outweighs the savings from reduced memory traffic, shifting decode attention from a memory bottleneck to a compute bottleneck. We present OptiDecode, a hybrid optoelectronic decode-attention accelerator that regenerates historical KV using free-space optics and computes attention digitally. Projection weights remain resident on optical tiles, exploiting reuse across historical tokens for high-throughput optical regeneration. Scaling to large models introduces two challenges. First, distributing weights across tiles requires sending the same activations to every head group, while each readout die produces only partial KV. Activation replay shares one set of electrical-to-optical converters across head groups without costly broadcast. In-situ attention avoids transferring partial KV from readout dies to reducers by computing on them locally and exchanging only partial scores, probabilities, and partial outputs. Second, processing an activation chunk through all dependent stages takes longer than one activation-fetch interval. Chunk pipelining overlaps successive chunks so that OptiDecode sustains the HBM activation-fetch rate. OptiDecode demonstrates 1.92-1.99x decode-attention speedup over an ideal GPU KV-read baseline at equal peak HBM bandwidth (A100-B200), for 32K-token contexts across evaluated 30B-175B MHA models, approaching the 2x upper bound from halving historical memory traffic.

entries.title: Power Scaling Across Link Utilization with GPAM-4 Signaling and Event-Driven Reception
entries.abstract: This work highlights the potential of combining event-based signaling with event-driven reception to achieve receiver power scaling across link utilization, without requiring wake-up, locking, or data-rate reconfiguration. The approach is demonstrated using the proposed four-level Gaussian pulse-amplitude modulation (GPAM-4) scheme and a corresponding event-driven receiver. By employing a resettable ring voltage-controlled oscillator (RRVCO) as its front end, the receiver achieves inherently event-driven symbol measurement, initiated directly by each received pulse. Symbols are decoded directly from the final RRVCO phase state, eliminating a counter-based back end. Simulated in 28-nm CMOS, the receiver power is evaluated across a 100× range of effective data rates—from 0.15 mW at the peak rate of 8 Gb/s, down to 2.5 μW under active/idle operation and 1.6 μW under data rate change at 80 Mb/s. The receiver thus achieves power reductions of 59.5× and 90.0×, while its energy per bit increases by only 1.68× and 1.11×, respectively.

entries.title: Towards Self-Organizing Channel Coding in 6G-Enabled IoT Networks: Trends, Cognitive Architectures, and Open Challenges
entries.abstract: The sixth-generation (6G) of wireless communication is designed to facilitate distributed edge intelligence, ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC), and massive machine-type communications (mMTC), all of which have the potential to revolutionize the Internet of Things (IoT). Autonomous vehicles, swarm robotics, XR, and industrial automation are IoT-centric 6G applications with demanding requirements; developing efficient, adaptive, and reliable channel coding methods is crucial to realizing this goal. This study explores the adaptation of various channel coding schemes to distributed IoT scenarios in 6G networks, covering both established and developing schemes, including LDPC, Turbo, Polar, and Fountain codes. We evaluate the relevance of recent developments to decentralized IoT designs, including AIassisted cognitive coding, neural network-based decoding, adaptive and context-aware coding, quantum and reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) coding. We further propose CACADe-6G, a cognitive architecture for adaptive channel coding; our evaluation shows that its principal benefit over simpler adaptive baselines lies in reduced switching overhead and energy consumption, rather than a guaranteed reduction in bit error rate relative to a memoryless threshold comparator. We compare different channel coding schemes with respect to latency, energy, and reliability requirements, and highlight important use cases. Findings from this study reveal current research gaps and identify potential future directions for coding in intelligent, large-scale IoT systems, aiming to guide future research and support the deployment of 6G-enabled IoT technologies.

entries.title: From Sensors to Silicon: Causal Cross-Layer Self-Healing Edge AI for Secure and Energy-Adaptive IoT Systems
entries.abstract: The migration of artificial intelligence from centralized cloud infrastructure to resource-constrained Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices reduces communication latency and improves data locality, but it also tightly couples sensing quality, inference behavior, microarchitectural activity, hardware reliability, security, and energy management within the same physical node. Existing edge-intelligence solutions predominantly address these dimensions in isolation, making it difficult to determine whether an observed degradation originates from sensor malfunction, data-distribution shift, malicious execution, hardware faults, or resource and thermal stress. This paper presents a causal cross-layer self-healing Edge-AI framework that continuously observes synchronized telemetry spanning sensor health, inference uncertainty, processor hardware-performance counters, accelerator and memory activity, power and thermal state, and communication conditions. A temporally informed causal reasoning engine estimates the most probable origin of abnormal behavior and quantifies diagnostic uncertainty, including under concurrent perturbations.

entries.title: EEGHyena2: Fixation-Inspired Joint Lexical-Grammatical Conditional Random Field for Interpretable EEG-to-Text Decoding
entries.abstract: A sentence is built from words that carry lexical meaning and grammatical roles, and brain activity during reading reflects both. Current EEG-to-text decoders, however, let a large language model (LLM) propose and order the words, so fluent output can reflect the LLM's prior more than the recorded EEG. In this study, we asked whether fixation-linked EEG carries lexical and grammatical evidence during natural reading and how a decoder can use such evidence. Fixation-related potential analyses showed that content and function words differ reliably in group-averaged EEG but only weakly in single words. We therefore propose EEGHyena2, a structured decoder in which a bidirectional encoder inspired by StripedHyena 2 feeds a semantic head that ranks a fixed lexicon and a part-of-speech (POS) head that predicts grammatical categories; a joint word-POS conditional random field (CRF) scores a restricted candidate lattice, and a frozen Llama-2 scores the candidates in context. On two natural-reading corpora, ZuCo and ROAMM, it matched the state-of-the-art method on BLEU-1 (21.4 vs 21.3), exceeded it on ROUGE-1 F1 (23.3 vs 20.3), lowered the character error rate on ROAMM (75.3% vs 84.7%) and decoded each recording about 3-10 times faster than LLM candidate search. The CRF learned transitions that mirror English syntax, and the encoder drew local context from its convolutions and distant context from attention. Decoders can thus pool weak word-level EEG evidence across the sentence through explicit lexical and grammatical structure, with the language model adjudicating among candidates rather than generating them, which lowers decoding cost and keeps decisions inspectable.

entries.title: Instructor-designed AI improves learning in a randomized trial across 19 universities
entries.abstract: Universities are alarmed by recent evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) can undermine learning, with students prescribed generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools performing worse. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities over three semesters, we tested whether AI designed by frontline instructors can improve learning. We encouraged instructors to design AI solutions they believed would best help their students. Drawing on their unique knowledge of their classes and students, the instructors created a wide array of innovations. We show that these instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning, measured by AI-proof assessments (proctored, in-person examinations). We found no change in student engagement, measured by course activity records, or satisfaction, measured by course evaluations. Our findings demonstrate that AI can improve student learning when its adoption is frontline-driven, with instructors empowered to design and refine AI solutions for their own classrooms.
